title: Avionics Electrical Technician
tagline: AETs inspect, service, maintain, troubleshoot, and repair aircraft electronic systems.
overview: AETs inspect, troubleshoot, and repair aircraft avionics and electrical systems, including power generation, batteries, flight control components, and landing gear. You'll also fly as an aircrew, performing duties like navigator, sensor and radio operation, or hoist operation. AETs are typically assigned to Coast Guard air stations.
requirements: Are you excited to fly?
Are you able to meet aircrew physical standards, including vision?
Are you good at practical math problems?
Are you interested in electrical systems?
training: AETs receive 24 weeks of blended on-the-job training at one of 26 Coast Guard air stations, in addition to in-class training at the Aviation Technical Training Center in Elizabeth City, NC. You will learn about aircraft systems, radar theory, aircraft communications, electrical theory, and troubleshooting.
Advanced aircraft electrical, engine, and airframe specific training, as well as advanced training in helicopter operations.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Aviation Technology program is available to the AET rating.

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard aircraft electronics and electrical systems working, then flies on them as aircrew.
ai.dayToDay:
Most of your time is at an air station hangar, with a multimeter and wiring diagrams, chasing faults in radios, radar, flight controls, generators and landing gear systems. When you're not on the hangar floor you may be flying as aircrew 
s
navigating, working sensors and radios, or running the rescue hoist. The pace follows the aircraft: routine inspections and paperwork, punctuated by launches that can't wait.
ai.funFact: The Aviation Technical Training Center at Elizabeth City, North Carolina, is the hub of Coast Guard aviation maintenance training, and AETs do on-the-job training across 26 air stations.
goodFitIf: enjoy electrical troubleshooting
want to fly as aircrew
can meet aircrew vision standards
are comfortable with practical math

title: Aviation Maintenance Technician
tagline: AMTs inspect, maintain, and troubleshoot aircraft engines, propellers, and airframes systems.
overview: AMTs inspect, maintain, troubleshoot, and repair aircraft mechanical systems, including engines, powertrains, and hydraulics. You'll service structural parts of the aircraft, including fuselages, wings, rotor blades, and flight control surfaces. You'll also fly as an aircrew, performing duties like loadmaster, dropmaster, or helicopter flight mechanic. AMTs are typically assigned to Coast Guard air stations.
requirements: Are you excited to fly?
Are you able to meet aircrew physical standards, including vision?
Are you good at practical math problems?
Are you interested in mechanical systems?
training: AMTs receive 20 weeks of blended on-the-job training at one of 26 Coast Guard air stations, in addition to in-class training at the Aviation Technical Training Center in Elizabeth City, NC. You will learn about aircraft systems, metal work, composite repair, electrical theory and troubleshooting, and paint applications.
Advanced composite repair, aircraft systems, and airframe specific training, as well as advanced training in helicopter rescue operations.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Aviation Technology program is available to the AMT rating.
civilianJobs: FAA Certified Aircraft Mechanic or Aircraft Inspector Authorization

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard helicopters and planes flying — engines, hydraulics, airframes — and flies on them as aircrew.
ai.dayToDay: You're based at an air station, working in a hangar on engines, powertrains, hydraulics, rotor blades and control surfaces, with inspections and troubleshooting filling most shifts. The other half of the job is in the air: AMTs fly as aircrew, working the hoist as a helicopter flight mechanic or handling loads as a loadmaster or dropmaster. Pace swings between steady scheduled maintenance and getting an aircraft fixed and airborne because a case has come in.
ai.funFact: The Aviation Technical Training Center in Elizabeth City, North Carolina trains the whole fleet's aviation maintainers, and AMTs can go on to the Aviation Technology degree programme from there.
goodFitIf: enjoy taking machines apart
are comfortable flying regularly
can meet aircrew vision standards
like practical maths and troubleshooting

title: Aviation Survival Technician
tagline: ASTs are specialized rescue swimmers who save lives, provide emergency medical support, and maintain survival equipment.
overview: ASTs are the Coast Guard’s specialized rescue swimmers, equipped with the survival training and experience necessary to keep themselves and others alive at sea or on land. With the gear you maintain, you'll fly on Coast Guard helicopters into a range of challenging situations, from emergencies at sea to floods on land to cliff-side rescues. AST tasks require the highest degree of physical fitness. ASTs are typically assigned to Coast Guard air stations.
requirements: Are you physically and mentally fit?
Are you extremely comfortable in the water?
Are you able to excel under stress?
Are you passionate about saving others?
training: ASTs receive a 22-week rating course that includes a 7-week EMT course to earn the National Registry of Emergency Medical Technician (NREMT) certification, a 10-week rescue swimmer course learning helicopter rescue procedures, and a 5-week aviation life support technician course learning the fundamentals of inspections and maintenance of aviation life support equipment.
Advanced helicopter rescue and operational fitness training, as well as survival instructor resident courses.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may be available.
civilianJobs: Commercial Aircraft Life Support Equipment Technician
Lifeguard, Ski Patrol, or Other Recreational Protective Service Worker

ai.blurb: Jumps from Coast Guard helicopters to rescue people from the sea, floods and cliffs, and treats their injuries.
ai.dayToDay: Most days are spent at an air station: inspecting and repairing survival gear, parachutes and life rafts, training in the pool or gym, and standing duty waiting for a call. When the call comes, you're in the water or on a hoist cable with a flight crew, often in weather that made someone else need rescuing. Physical training isn't optional extra — it's a core part of the job, and you work closely with pilots, flight mechanics and other ASTs.
ai.funFact: ASTs earn a National Registry EMT certification during their 22-week rating course, so a rescue swimmer is also a qualified medic.
goodFitIf: you're genuinely at home in water
you stay calm when things go wrong
you'll keep training hard for years
you like fixing gear as well as using it

title: Boatswain’s Mate
tagline: BMs are experts in all things navigation and seamanship.
overview: BMs are experts at navigating vessels and have the most command leadership opportunities of any rating. When operating a boat as coxswain, you'll be in charge of executing the mission and be responsible for the safety of your crew members. You'll also have a chance to train as a law enforcement officer to conduct maritime boardings. BMs can be found at nearly every operational unit.
requirements: Are you comfortable as a leader?
Are you attentive to detail?
Are you excited to operate small boats?
Are you interested in law enforcement?
training: BMs receive a 14-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in seamanship and navigation.
Advanced maritime navigation training and tactical law enforcement training.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may be available.
civilianJobs: Captain, Mate, or Pilot of Water Vessels
First-line Supervisor of Material-moving Machine and Vehicle Operators
Schedule Development or Personnel Management Specialist

ai.blurb: Drives Coast Guard boats, runs deck operations, and leads crews on search, rescue and law enforcement missions.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens on or alongside the water — small boats, cutter decks, piers and station watchrooms. You'll handle lines and anchors, maintain gear, stand watch, and in time qualify as coxswain, meaning you command the boat and answer for the crew's safety. Many BMs also train as boarding officers, stopping and inspecting vessels at sea.
ai.funFact: Boatswain's Mate is one of the oldest ratings afloat, and the rating badge still shows crossed anchors — the trade predates the Coast Guard itself.
goodFitIf: You want command responsibility early
You like being on the water
Law enforcement work appeals
You notice small details others miss

title: Culinary Specialist
tagline: CSs are trained in all things food, from preparation to accounting and logistics.
overview: CSs keep Coast Guard crews fed by preparing meals to the highest standards of nutrition, taste, and food safety. Before the food even hits the pan, you'll be responsible for the intricate details of logistics, accounting, menu planning, and inventory management to keep pantries well stocked. You'll be trained in a variety of culinary arts to keep the menu fresh and morale high. CSs are typically assigned to galleys on cutters, ashore, or at VIP facilities.
requirements: Are you passionate about food?
Are you creative and resourceful?
Are you comfortable with math and accounting?
Are you customer service-focused?
training: CSs receive a 13-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in culinary fundamentals, advanced methods, and techniques.
Independent duty culinary service officer certification, advanced pastry and baking training, and advanced culinary skills training (ACF certified).

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Culinary Arts program is available to the CS rating.

ai.blurb: Cooks for Coast Guard crews and runs the food budget, ordering and inventory behind every meal.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens in a galley — on a cutter at sea, at a shore unit, or at a VIP facility — and it starts early, because breakfast doesn't wait. You plan menus, order and count stock, keep the accounts straight, then cook and serve for a crew that eats the same food three times a day and notices everything. On a small cutter you may be one of very few cooks, which means the quality of the meals, and a fair bit of the crew's mood, rests on you.
ai.funFact: Coast Guard culinary training runs 13 weeks in Petaluma, California, and advanced courses are certified by the American Culinary Federation — the same body that certifies civilian chefs.
goodFitIf: You cook well under time pressure
Numbers and inventory don't scare you
You like feeding people properly
You can improvise with what's aboard

title: Gunner’s Mate
tagline: GMs maintain firearms, from handguns to ship-mounted guns.
overview: GMs are responsible for all firearms and weapons systems, ammunition, and pyrotechnics in the Coast Guard. You'll be trained in mechanical, electronic, and hydraulic systems, as well as ammunition and pyrotechnics handling. GMs use, maintain, and train others on all Coast Guard small arms and shipboard weapons systems to ensure every unit's readiness to perform law enforcement and defense duties. GMs are assigned to a wide variety of units both afloat and ashore.
requirements: Are you comfortable with firearms?
Are you attentive to detail?
Are you inclined toward mechanics and math?
Are you interested in law enforcement or security?
training: GMs receive a 10-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in electronic and mechanical systems, as well as hydraulics.
Advanced training in weapons systems maintenance and small arms instruction.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may be available.

ai.blurb: Looks after every weapon in the Coast Guard, from sidearms to deck guns, and teaches others to shoot straight.
ai.dayToDay: Much of it is methodical bench work: stripping, inspecting and reassembling small arms, tracing faults in the electronics and hydraulics that drive shipboard mounts, and keeping careful account of ammunition and pyrotechnics. The rest is range time, running qualification shoots and coaching crews who need to stay current for boardings and law enforcement work. You could be aboard a cutter or in a shore armoury, working closely with boarding teams and the unit's gunner's mates.
ai.funFact: Gunner's mate is one of the oldest ratings at sea, dating back to the age of sail, when the gunner was responsible for the ship's powder as well as its cannon — today's GMs still answer for the magazine.
goodFitIf: You like taking mechanisms apart
You are meticulous about safety and paperwork
Teaching others appeals to you
Law enforcement work interests you

title: Machinery Technician
tagline: MKs are skilled in maintenance and repair of machinery such as hydraulics and engines.
overview: MKs are responsible for systems, including internal combustion engines, heating and ventilation, hydraulics, and basic electricity. With their intimate knowledge of ships systems, many MKs train to conduct law enforcement boardings. At smaller units, an MK is often the Engineering Petty Officer, who is responsible for the engineering department and equipment. MKs can be found at nearly every unit.
requirements: Are you a hands-on person?
Are you a problem solver?
Are you able to understand mechanics and schematics?
Are you drawn to practical mechanical experiences?
training: MKs receive a 13-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in basic mechanical and electrical theory and operation, as well as introduction to engine overhaul and maintenance.
Specific diesel engine and outboard engine training, as well as training in heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, hydraulics, law enforcement, leadership, and management.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Engineering Technology program is available to the MK rating.
civilianJobs: Supervisor of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard engines, hydraulics and ship systems running — and often helps board vessels for law enforcement.
ai.dayToDay: You work in engine rooms, machinery spaces and small-boat sheds: diesels, pumps, hydraulics, HVAC, basic electrical. Expect oily hands, troubleshooting against a schematic, and planned maintenance that has to be done whether or not the weather is cooperating. At a small station you may be the Engineering Petty Officer, running the whole engineering side, and many MKs also qualify for boarding teams.
ai.funFact: MKs are found at nearly every Coast Guard unit — cutters, small boat stations, shore facilities — which makes the rating one of the most widely spread in the service.
goodFitIf: You like taking machines apart
You read schematics without flinching
You want engineering and law enforcement
You don't mind dirty, practical work

title: Public Affairs Specialist
tagline: PAs are the link between the Coast Guard and the public, specializing in mass communications.
overview: PAs are public communications specialists. You'll write news releases, shoot still and video imagery, serve as a spokesperson to the media, and maintain official social media accounts and web content. You'll focus public awareness on important Coast Guard issues and respond to inquiries about Coast Guard actions. PAs are typically assigned to districts and large sectors.
requirements: Are you a skilled communicator?
Are you able to maintain poise under pressure?
Are you creative and self-motivated?
Are you interested in photography, videography, and social media?
training: PAs receive a 26-week rating course in Fort Meade, MD, with instruction in news writing, on-camera performance, photography, and videography.

FEMA incident command system (ICS) and public information officer (PIO) certifications. Advanced training in photojournalism, digital imagery, editing and design, media relations, and crisis communication.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Public Affairs Program is available to the PA rating.

ai.blurb: Writes the news releases, shoots the photos and video, and speaks to reporters about what the Coast Guard is doing.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens at a district or large sector office, writing stories, editing imagery and keeping official social media and web pages current. When something big happens — a rescue, a spill, a storm — you're the one fielding press calls and standing in front of a camera, often with incomplete information and a deadline. The rest of the time is quieter: ride-alongs, interviews with crews, photo assignments, and a lot of editing.
ai.funFact: PA training happens at Fort Meade, Maryland, home of the Defense Information School, where the military's writers, photographers and broadcasters from every service learn the trade side by side.
goodFitIf: you write clearly and fast
you stay calm on camera
you like photography and video
you can work without supervision

title: Storekeeper
tagline: SKs are skilled at logistics, purchasing, and contract management.
overview: SKs purchase the supplies that keep the Coast Guard running. From computers to spare parts for boats and aircraft, you'll handle logistics, track inventory, and account for funds. You'll become an expert in federal acquisitions procedures, contracting, government property management, and accounting. SKs are assigned to a wide variety of units ashore and afloat.
requirements: Are you organized?
Are you good with math and analytics?
Are you comfortable with computer software?
Are you a skilled communicator?
training: SKs receive an 8-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in procurement, shipping and receiving, inventory management, accounting, and records and reports.

Contract specialist, contracting officer, and contracting officer representative training. Certifications as defense financial manager, public accountant, logistics technician, logistics associate, production and inventory management, transportation professional, and accounts payable professional.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Financial Accounting and Contract Management Programs are available to the SK rating.
skills: Purchasing and contracting for an organization

ai.blurb: Buys and tracks everything the Coast Guard needs to operate, from laptops to spare parts for boats and aircraft.
ai.dayToDay: Mostly desk and storeroom work: raising purchase orders, checking deliveries against paperwork, keeping inventory straight and accounting for funds. You might be in a supply office ashore or squeezed into a storeroom aboard a cutter, dealing with crews who need a part today and vendors who say next month. Expect a lot of software, a lot of records, and a fair amount of chasing people.
ai.funFact: Storekeeper is one of the oldest job titles at sea — the term predates the Coast Guard itself, from the days when one person literally kept the ship's stores under lock and key.
goodFitIf: You like order and paperwork done properly
You're comfortable with numbers and software
You can chase people politely but firmly
You want transferable business qualifications

title: Yeoman
tagline: YNs specialize in military human resources issues, ranging from pay to travel and assignments.
overview: YNs are human relations problem-solvers, uniquely specialized to support the needs of the military. You'll assist with the hiring and separation of members, and manage personnel records to ensure pay and entitlements are correct. For members' major life events, from promotions to moves or even adding new dependents to the Coast Guard family, you'll make sure it happens seamlessly. YNs are assigned to a wide variety of units.
requirements: Are you organized?
Are you customer service-focused?
Are you comfortable with computer software?
training: YNs receive an 8-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in human resources, record management, payroll accounting, travel reimbursement, and personnel transfers.
Paralegal training.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Yeoman Business Administration and Management and Paralegal Studies Programs are available to the YN rating.

ai.blurb: Handles the Coast Guard's human resources — pay, orders, records, promotions and travel claims for everyone at the unit.
ai.dayToDay: Mostly office work at a cutter, air station, base or headquarters, in front of a computer and a counter where shipmates turn up with problems: a pay entitlement that didn't start, a move that needs orders, a new baby to enrol. The pace follows the calendar — transfer season, promotion cycles and payday bring surges. You deal with nearly everyone in the unit, often including the commanding officer, and you'll be expected to know the regulations well enough to give a straight answer.
ai.funFact: "Yeoman" is one of the oldest ratings afloat, borrowed from the Royal Navy, where the yeoman of the ship kept stores and records long before anyone had a computer to do it on.
goodFitIf: You like order and paperwork done right
You're patient with people's problems
You're comfortable learning software and rules
You want transferable office skills

title: Operations Specialist
tagline: OSs provide 24/7 communication and coordination to execute missions.
overview: OSs are the Coast Guard's preeminent emergency managers. You'll provide situational awareness, manage information, and develop plans for missions ranging from search and rescue to law enforcement, national defense, and more. From command centers ashore and at sea, OSs communicate with boaters in distress, develop search patterns, and guide Coast Guard units to assist. OSs are typically assigned to sectors, districts, and cutters.
requirements: Are you calm under pressure?
Are you attentive to detail?
Are you interested in coordinating response actions?
Are you punctual?
training: OSs receive a 13-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in handling classified information, navigation, communications systems, and search and rescue planning.
Tactical action officer training, command duty officer training, and air direction controller training, along with training in electronic warfare and emergency management.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Emergency Management program is available to the OS rating.

ai.blurb: Takes the distress call, works out where the boat is, and directs the rescue from a command centre.
ai.dayToDay: You work watches in a command centre ashore at a sector or district, or in the operations room of a cutter, surrounded by radios, radar and charts. Most of a shift is routine monitoring and logging; then a mayday comes in and you're questioning a frightened caller, plotting a search pattern and vectoring boats and helicopters onto it. You work closely with watch supervisors, boat crews, aircrews and other agencies, and you handle classified material.
ai.funFact: Search planning is a real science — drift models account for wind and current to work out where a person or boat has moved since they went missing, which is why OSs train for 13 weeks at Petaluma before standing watch.
goodFitIf: You stay calm when others panic
You like radios, charts and radar
You can hold a detail-heavy watch
Shift work doesn't bother you

title: Maritime Enforcement Specialist
tagline: MEs are technical experts and trainers for law enforcement operations.
overview: While many ratings participate in law enforcement, MEs are the Coast Guard's specialists. You'll lead and train your crew's boarding teams and maintain the unit's law enforcement equipment. When situations demand the highest risk tactics, like helicopter insertion or opposed boardings, deployable specialized forces of MEs get the call. MEs are typically assigned to cutters, boat stations, and specialized units.
requirements: Are you passionate about law enforcement?
Are you physically and mentally fit?
Are you able to excel under stress?
Are you confident and assertive?
training: MEs receive a 10-week rating course in Charleston, SC, with instruction in maritime law enforcement, force protection, weapons, and coastal security operations.
Advanced training in security tactics, police academy, emergency vehicle operation.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may be available.
civilianJobs: Local, State, and Federal Law Enforcement

ai.blurb: Coast Guard's law enforcement specialist — boards vessels, trains boarding teams and handles the highest-risk takedowns at sea.
ai.dayToDay: You'll be on cutters, at boat stations or with specialised units, running and training the boarding teams that stop and search vessels. A lot of the job is routine: maintaining weapons and law enforcement gear, drilling your crew, standing security watches. Then there are the boardings themselves, which can mean climbing onto a moving vessel, or for deployable units, fast-roping in from a helicopter.
ai.funFact: The ME rating is relatively young — it was created in the 2000s, when the Coast Guard decided its law enforcement and port security work had grown specialised enough to need a rating of its own.
goodFitIf: You want a policing career
You stay calm under pressure
You like teaching and leading others
You're comfortable being physically tested

title: Afloat Officer
tagline: Afloat officers operate a multi-mission fleet of Coast Guard cutters to execute all assigned missions worldwide.
overview:
As a “cutterman,” you’ll join the oldest career in the service, safely navigating cutter ships and leading your crew in enforcing federal laws and completing challenging missions in unforgiving environments.
You’ll start out by leading enlisted members and learning the fundamentals of seamanship. As you progress, you’ll be given more responsibility to perform more complex missions on larger vessels.
Ship assignments typically last two years, including one year at sea. In between sea duty assignments, you’ll focus on a secondary specialty and gain advanced training and education.
requirements: You can start your career as a cutterman through a general commissioning source like Officer Candidate School and choosing your first and subsequent assignments in the specialty.

extra.Law Enforcement Cutters: The Coast Guard’s multi-mission “white hull” cutters use their superior communications, speed, embarked boats, and aircraft to perform missions critical to national interests—such as drug interdiction, stopping human trafficking, and policing global fisheries.
extra.Waterways Management Cutters: The Coast Guard’s “black hull” buoy tenders and domestic icebreakers ensure the safe operation of our nation’s critical commercial waterways. You’ll become an expert in servicing and positioning the buoys that safely guide mariners into port and break safe channels in the ice in the Great Lakes and northeast waterways.
extra.Polar Operations: The Coast Guard has the only icebreakers in federal service that can operate at the poles. These “red hull” icebreakers can break through pack ice over 20 feet thick, providing essential logistics for the U.S. presence in Antarctica, conducting scientific measurements around the North Pole, and more.

ai.blurb: Commissioned officer who navigates Coast Guard cutters and leads their crews on law enforcement, buoy tending and icebreaking missions.
ai.dayToDay: You live aboard a ship for long stretches — standing watch on the bridge, navigating, and running a division of enlisted crew who do the actual deck, engineering and boarding work. Depending on the hull you draw, a day might mean chasing smugglers in the Caribbean, hauling a multi-tonne buoy onto the deck, or grinding through pack ice. Sea assignments usually run around two years with roughly a year of that actually underway; ashore, you build a second specialty and take further training.
ai.funFact: Coast Guard cutters are colour-coded by job: white hulls do law enforcement, black hulls tend buoys and break domestic ice, and red hulls are the polar icebreakers — the only ships in federal service able to work at both poles.
goodFitIf: you don't mind months at sea
you like leading people early
navigation and ship handling appeal
cold, wet weather doesn't bother you

title: Aviation Officer
tagline: Coast Guard aviators pilot airplanes and helicopters in challenging conditions to save lives and complete a multitude of missions.
overview: Did you know the U.S. Coast Guard has the highest percentage of officers that are pilots out of any U.S. military service? As a Coast Guard aviator, you’ll fly in challenging, high-risk environments—such as rescuing people in distress, stopping smugglers, or monitoring illegal activities.
requirements: If you have prior military flight experience as a pilot, you can join the Coast Guard through the Direct Commission Aviation program and immediately begin flying.

If you don’t have military flight experience as a pilot, you can join through a general commissioning source such as Officer Candidate School and earn flight school as your first assignment or apply and be selected for flight school later in your career.
If you are a CSPI Officer Trainee, you can enter flight school through the Wilkes Flight Initiative.
training: When you’re selected for flight school, you’ll attend Naval Flight School at Naval Air Station Pensacola, FL. It takes approximately two years for you to earn your wings, as you cycle through:
Initial Flight Screening (IFS), where you’ll become familiar with flying and make sure it’s a fit for you.

Aviation Pre-flight Indoctrination (API), where you’ll learn basic aerodynamics, aviation weather, air navigation, flight rules and regulations, aircraft engines and systems, and how flight affects the human body.

Primary Flight Training, where you’ll do extensive training in simulators and aircraft. Depending on your interests and available opportunities, you’ll be assigned to either the fixed-wing aircraft or helicopter subspecialty.
The Secondary Phase of Flight School is either in Pensacola, FL, for helicopters, or Corpus Christi, TX, for fixed-wing aircraft.

After you earn your wings, you’ll be assigned to an air station and attend an airframe-specific course at Aviation Training Center in Mobile, AL, to qualify for the MH-60 Jayhawk, the MH-65 Dolphin, the HC-130 Hercules, or the HC-144 Ocean Sentry. You’ll return once a year for a one-week proficiency course in your airframe.

extra.Aeronautical Engineering:
Aeronautical engineers are vital to Coast Guard aircraft and avionics systems acquisition, planning, design, operation, maintenance, and alteration. Within this specialty, you can choose from three master’s degree paths:
• Avionics/Project Management: You’ll learn to manage technology upgrade and modification projects.
• Structures Specialists: You’ll approve structural repairs, aircraft maintenance procedures, and corrosion mitigation processes.
• STEM MBA: You’ll provide engineering support, logistics, and oversight of depot-level maintenance. As an aeronautical engineer, you’ll maintain your flying qualifications.
extra.Aviation Career:
You can expect to gain initial experience as a co-pilot and eventually earn the title of aircraft commander. Throughout your aviation career, you’ll experience search-and-rescue, law enforcement, and other Coast Guard missions. Once you gain leadership and operational skills, you may be selected for command of an air station. You’ll also be encouraged to apply for sponsored graduate school programs to broaden your expertise outside of the cockpit, such as:
• Aeronautical Engineering – Avionics (Project Management)
• Aeronautical Engineering – (STEM MBA)
• Aeronautical Engineering – (Structures)
• Aviation Safety Systems
• Aviation Technology
extra.Related Enlisted Careers:
• Aviation Maintenance Technician
• Avionics Electrical Technician

ai.blurb: Flies Coast Guard helicopters and aeroplanes on search-and-rescue, law enforcement and patrol missions, often in foul weather.
ai.dayToDay: You're based at an air station, flying one airframe — the MH-60 Jayhawk, MH-65 Dolphin, HC-130 Hercules or HC-144 Ocean Sentry — with a small crew you train with constantly. Much of the work is briefings, maintenance checks, currency flights and duty standby; then a call comes in and you're launching over water in conditions most aircraft stay home for. You start as a co-pilot, build hours, and eventually qualify as aircraft commander, with command of an air station possible later.
ai.funFact: The Coast Guard has the highest percentage of officers who are pilots of any US military service, and its aviators train alongside the Navy at Naval Air Station Pensacola.
goodFitIf: You want flying as the whole job
You stay calm in bad weather
You can commit to years of training
You like small, tight-knit crews

title: Engineering & C5I Officer
tagline: Engineers maintain physical readiness of the fleet and its command, control, communications, computers, cyber, and intelligence (C5I) functions.
requirements: If you have prior education and experience, you can enter the field through the DCE program or through a general source like OCS, and choose assignments in the specialty, although it helps greatly to have a STEM degree.

extra.Naval Engineering:
As a naval engineer, you’ll be part of one of the Coast Guard’s largest programs as you execute and oversee the design, construction, acquisition, operation, maintenance, and sustainment of cutters and boats.
You’ll start your career learning basic shipboard engineering fundamentals in the engineering department of a cutter. Next, you’ll have shore assignment focusing on ship maintenance management and contract officer certification. You’ll also have the chance to earn a fully funded master’s degree and return to sea for a second afloat assignment as the engineer officer on a large cutter.
The naval engineering specialty pairs well with the afloat operations specialty and you can easily compete for additional afloat opportunities, including command.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Machinery Technician
• Electrician's Mate
extra.Civil Engineering:
Civil engineers manage the entire life cycle of the Coast Guard’s shore infrastructure, including planning, budgeting, design, construction, commissioning, operation, maintenance, and divestiture. Most first assignments are hands-on at a civil engineering unit, facilities design and construction center, or facilities engineering office. As you gain experience, you’ll transition to management-focused roles.
This flexible subspecialty encourages officers to pursue out-of-specialty tours, career-broadening assignments, and graduate studies in civil engineering, ocean engineering, and engineering management.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Damage Controlman
extra.Cyberspace:
As an expert in cyber, you’ll gain the training, clearance, and qualifications to build, secure, operate, defend, and protect Coast Guard and U.S. cyberspace resources. You’ll develop and enhance your skills through on-the-job-training and experience, as well as graduate school opportunities and out-of-specialty assignments.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Information Systems Technician
• Electronics Technician

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard ships, shore bases and computer networks working, from engine rooms to cyber defence.
ai.dayToDay: Depending on your subspecialty, you might spend your first tour in a cutter's engineering department learning how the propulsion and systems actually behave at sea, or at a shore unit managing construction projects and maintenance contracts, or working cyber defence with a security clearance. Expect a mix of grease-under-the-fingernails troubleshooting early on and budget, contract and management work later. You'll work alongside enlisted machinery technicians, electricians, damage controlmen and IT specialists who know the equipment intimately.
ai.funFact: Naval engineering is one of the Coast Guard's largest programs, and it pairs so naturally with afloat operations that engineers can compete for cutter command.
goodFitIf: you like systems and how they fail
a STEM degree appeals to you
you want graduate school funded
you'd mix sea time with shore projects

title: Healthcare Officer
tagline: These officers ensure the delivery of essential health services to active-duty Coast Guard members at base clinics, on temporary deployments, and in remote or challenging environments.
overview:
Do you want to practice your medical specialty in a fast-paced, patient-focused environment? Consider this — in the Coast Guard, medical providers are able to concentrate on clinical practice without the hassle of maintaining a private business. Your patients will almost exclusively be active-duty military members whose medical readiness is critical to enabling the success of Coast Guard missions. Plus, you’ll enjoy both the tangible and intangible benefits of military service.
For Coast Guard officers with no medical training, there are opportunities to enter the healthcare field by competing for advanced education as a physician, physician assistant, or medical administrator.
requirements: If you’re an enlisted health services technician or junior officer from a general source such as Officer Candidate School (OCS), you can apply for opportunities to complete the Interservice Physician Assistant Program (IPAP). You can become a medical administrator by beginning your career through a general commissioning source like OCS and competing for post-graduate education opportunities.

If you have prior education and credentials as a provider, you can enter the field through the Direct Commission Health Services Officer or Direct Commission Physician Assistant programs. To pursue assignment as a detailed USPHS provider, contact the USCG Program Manager.

extra.Physicians & Physician Assistants:
Through a combination of direct employment and partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS), the Coast Guard employs board certified/board eligible primary care physicians who are typically residency-trained in family medicine, internal medicine, or emergency medicine. Positions also exist in psychiatry, aerospace, occupational, preventive medicine, and pediatrics.
If you meet the relevant medical standards and desire a more operational experience, you could qualify for additional training to become a flight surgeon, aviation physician assistant, or hyperbaric medical officer.
extra.Dentistry: Coast Guard dentists are employed through a combination of partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS) and direct employment. As a licensed dentist, you’ll provide general dental care for active-duty members of the Coast Guard or other military services. Positions also exist in endodontics, exodontia, and oral and maxillofacial surgery.
extra.Psychology & Social Work: The Coast Guard employs licensed psychologists and social workers through a combination of direct employment and partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS). Your work would include providing assessment, diagnosis, and treatment for mental health disorders, making fitness for duty determinations, and supporting the medical board process for retaining or separating members. Additional opportunities exist in aeromedical psychology.
extra.Environmental Health: Environmental health officers are employed through a combination of partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS) and direct employment. Examples of the work you may see include epidemiological surveillance, disease prevention, radiological health, industrial hygiene, food safety, injury prevention and education, and emergency preparedness. During natural disasters and other emergencies, you’ll protect Coast Guard personnel from environmental threats and help communities recover.
extra.Pharmacy: Through a combination of direct employment and partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS), the Coast Guard employs licensed pharmacists. While primarily assigned to Coast Guard clinics, you’ll find a wide variety of work—including caring for patients; reviewing, approving, and monitoring new drugs; and assisting in public health emergencies.
extra.Nursing: Nurses who serve in the Coast Guard through either direct employment or partnership with the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS) will typically work with multiple clinics across a multi-state area. Regional Nurse Case Managers complement other providers to ensure that Coast Guard members receive appropriate care and can return to mission-ready as quickly as possible.
extra.Medical Administration: Officers in this specialty manage and administer healthcare facilities such as Coast Guard clinics. You’ll supervise assigned enlisted health services technicians, manage the clinic’s budget, and coordinate care to ensure the medical and dental readiness of all military personnel in your area. At the senior level, you’ll manage entire regions, programs for health, safety, and work-life, or develop policy for programs.

ai.blurb: Doctors, dentists, nurses, pharmacists and health administrators who keep Coast Guard members fit for duty.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens in a Coast Guard base clinic, seeing a patient population that is almost entirely young, active-duty people — so a lot of primary care, dental work, mental health assessments and fitness-for-duty calls rather than running a business. You work alongside enlisted health services technicians, and depending on your specialty you might cover several clinics across a multi-state region, deploy temporarily, or support communities after a hurricane. Some providers go operational as flight surgeons, aviation PAs or hyperbaric medical officers.
ai.funFact: Many Coast Guard medical providers aren't Coast Guard at all — they're commissioned officers of the U.S. Public Health Service, one of the eight uniformed services, detailed to the Coast Guard.
goodFitIf: You already hold clinical credentials
You'd rather treat patients than bill them
You want medicine with an operational edge
You like a young, healthy patient population

title: Prevention Officer
tagline: Prevention officers exercise Coast Guard authorities to protect the environment, provide security, and prevent casualties to people and property.
overview:
Do you like to solve complex problems, lead, improve systems and processes, and serve others by ensuring their safety? If so, consider the prevention career path. You’ll learn about maritime transportation systems, and set and enforce standards for maritime safety and security.
As you progress, you’ll work toward becoming a prevention department head responsible for coordinating all prevention operations at a Coast Guard sector. With more experience, you’ll rise to command of a Coast Guard sector.
requirements: You can enter the prevention specialty by beginning your career through a general commissioning source like OCS and choosing assignments in the specialty. Maritime Academy Direct Commission Officer Program graduates are especially well-suited for this field.

extra.Vessel Inspections: A common first assignment, you’ll master safety, security, and environmental compliance requirements for vessels of all types. You’ll also certify U.S. commercial and foreign vessels for compliance with U.S. regulations and international treaties that ensure the safety of the maritime transportation system and protect the environment.
extra.Marine Investigations: When accidents occur at sea, you’ll determine the cause of the event by conducting interviews and evaluating evidence, collecting the facts of the casualty, determining the need for fines or criminal prosecution, and making recommendations to prevent future incidents.
extra.Waterways Management: You’ll ensure access to navigable waterways, and promote safe and environmentally sound marine transportation systems by managing waterway infrastructure and vessel movements, communicating waterway conditions, and exercising authority of the Coast Guard Captain of the Port. Assignments include vessel traffic service centers, marine safety units, navigation centers, or international ice patrol.
extra.Port and Facility Safety and Security: You’ll oversee compliance with regulations that keep shoreside port facilities operating safely. From explosives and hazardous cargo to shipping containers, your enforcement efforts will mitigate threats to workers, the port, and your community.
extra.Marine Safety Engineering: You’ll be a technical expert in all aspects of commercial vessel and offshore safety and design, reviewing vessel plans for compliance, providing technical advice to the field during casualties, and developing standards to improve safety.

ai.blurb: Inspects ships and ports, investigates marine accidents, and enforces the safety, security and environmental rules that keep commercial shipping honest.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens in ports — climbing through the engine rooms and cargo holds of commercial ships, walking waterfront facilities that handle hazardous cargo, or sitting in a vessel traffic centre watching movements on a busy harbour. You'll spend a good share of time on paperwork too: inspection reports, plan reviews, casualty investigations built from interviews and evidence. Colleagues include ship masters, port operators, engineers and Marine Science Technicians, many of whom know their vessels far better than you do at first.
ai.funFact: One possible assignment is the International Ice Patrol, founded after the Titanic sank and still tracking icebergs in the North Atlantic today.
goodFitIf: You enjoy picking apart complex systems
Regulations and standards genuinely interest you
You like ships and commercial shipping
You can hold a line politely under pressure

title: Response Officer
tagline: Response officers control shore-based assets to save those in distress, enforce maritime laws, and manage disasters.
overview:
As an officer on the response career path, you’ll gain the skills and experience to manage and execute shore-based Coast Guard operations, like search and rescue, law enforcement, coastal security, environmental response, and emergency management.
As you progress in your career, you’ll get experience in additional subspecialties. At the mid-career level, you’ll likely have an assignment as the Response Department Head at a Coast Guard Sector in charge of all Response mission areas. Eventually, you’ll be able to compete for command of a Coast Guard Sector.
requirements: Start your response career through a general commissioning source like Officer Candidate School and choose assignments in the specialty.

extra.Search and Rescue Coordination: You’ll stand watch in a Coast Guard Command Center and manage the response to distress calls, and plan search patterns to locate missing mariners.
extra.Maritime Law Enforcement: You’ll perform missions for coastal security, living marine resources law enforcement, and general law enforcement, and get trained in the use of force, tactical procedures, and defensive tactics.
extra.Boat Forces Operations: You’ll get certifications for the Coast Guard’s shore-based small boats, and be responsible for their safe navigation and operations as you conduct search and rescue and law enforcement missions.
extra.Marine Environmental Response: You’ll become an expert on federal environmental law and regulations and be responsible for directing the removal and mitigation of oil and hazardous substances from the marine environment.
extra.Deployable Specialized Forces: You’ll work closely with the Department of Defense and be available to deploy anywhere in the U.S. on short notice as the premier force for high-risk maritime operations, such as security threats, helicopter insertions, opposed boardings, and close-quarters combat techniques.
extra.Emergency Management: You’ll help plan and coordinate response to major disasters with federal and state agency partners, local organizations, and your port’s maritime industry focusing on port security and readiness, as well as environmental protection.
extra.Related Enlisted Careers:
• Boatswain’s Mate
• Maritime Enforcement Specialist
• Operations Specialist
• Marine Science Technician

ai.blurb: Runs Coast Guard operations from shore — search and rescue, law enforcement, oil spills and disaster response.
ai.dayToDay: Much of the work happens in a Sector command centre or a small boat station rather than at sea for months: standing watch, taking distress calls, plotting search patterns, and deciding which boats and aircraft go where. Other days you're out on a shore-based small boat doing boardings, or managing an oil spill cleanup alongside state agencies and port industry. You work with Boatswain's Mates, Operations Specialists and Marine Science Technicians, and the pace swings from paperwork to all-hands-on-deck with little warning.
ai.funFact: Search planning is a genuine science — the Coast Guard uses computer models of wind and current drift to work out where a missing person is likely to have ended up, and the search area is reassessed as each hour passes.
goodFitIf: stay calm when a call comes in
like planning as much as doing
want to lead teams early
are drawn to law and regulation

title: Support Officer
tagline: The Coast Guard’s support specialties—including finance, intelligence, law, and reserve component management—are vital to our operations and offer great career opportunities.

extra.Financial Management:
As a financial management specialist, your career will focus on budgeting, financial analysis, accounting operations, internal controls, audit readiness, and supply and inventory management. Assignments are typically located at headquarters, district staffs, bases, training centers, and service centers.
How to Enter the Specialty
You can begin your career as a financial management specialist through a general commissioning source like Officer Candidate School and choosing assignments in the specialty, or by obtaining an advanced degree (e.g., MBA or MPA).
Related Enlisted Careers
• Storekeeper
extra.Intelligence:
Intelligence officers collect, analyze, process, and disseminate intelligence in support of the Coast Guard’s missions. At the strategic level, intelligence informs global force laydown, acquisitions, partnerships, and interagency activities.
Your assignments may include counterintelligence, cryptologic groups, cyber, interagency, or criminal investigations. You’ll gain increased responsibility as your career progresses, and develop your decision-making and leadership skills by leading a larger branch or division or pursuing a post-graduate program.
You may also seek to broaden into a second specialty such as cyber, finance, or human resources.
How to Enter the Specialty
If you have prior education and experience, you can enter the field through the DCIO program, or through a general source like Officer Candidate School and choose assignments in the specialty.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Intelligence Specialist
extra.Law:
As a member of the Coast Guard legal program (CGJAG), you’ll engage in every facet of mission support and deliver legal advice across the full spectrum of Coast Guard operations. To receive a CGJAG assignment, you must apply and provide satisfactory evidence of law school graduation and bar admission.
Additional information regarding a career in the CGJAG can be found here.
How to Enter the Specialty
If you have prior education and credentials, you can enter the field through the Direct Commission Lawyer program, or you can enter through a general source like Officer Candidate School and complete advanced education opportunities in the field.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Yeoman
extra.Reserve Component Manager:
As a reserve component manager (RCM), you’ll organize, recruit, train, and provide administrative support for Coast Guard reservists. You’ll be responsible for making sure the reserve force is deployment-ready and capable of augmenting the active-duty workforce during anticipated shortages.
How to Enter the Specialty
You can enter the specialty if you were commissioned through a general source such as Officer Candidate School or the Selected Reserve Direct Commission (SRDC) program, and applying to a competitive panel for selection to the specialty.
Related Enlisted Careers
• Yeoman

ai.blurb: Coast Guard officer working in finance, intelligence, law, or reserve management—the staff work that keeps operations running.
ai.dayToDay: Mostly office work at headquarters, district staffs, bases and service centres rather than on a cutter. Depending on the specialty you might be building budgets and chasing audit readiness, writing intelligence assessments for operational commanders, advising on legal questions across every Coast Guard mission, or making sure reservists are trained and ready to be called up. You work alongside enlisted storekeepers, yeomen and intelligence specialists, and with other federal agencies.
ai.funFact: Coast Guard lawyers are part of the CGJAG programme, and you can commission directly as one through the Direct Commission Lawyer route—provided you've finished law school and passed a bar.
goodFitIf: You already have a professional degree
You like analysis over deck work
You want a career with civilian parallels
Detail and paperwork don't scare you

title: Cyber Mission Specialist
tagline: CMSs defend Coast Guard and maritime networks against a full range of cyber threats.
overview: CMSs protect Coast Guard networks and the Marine Transportation System from cyber risks. You'll detect and disrupt adversary activities with full spectrum cybersecurity operations. Your vigilance and actions will contain and minimize threats, ensuring continuity of Coast Guard and national defense missions. CMSs are typically assigned to dedicated cyber shore units.
requirements: Are you vigilant?
Are you comfortable with computer software?
Are you excited to solve challenging technical problems?
Are you attentive to detail?
training: CMSs attend the Navy’s 27-week Joint Cyber Analysis Course (JCAC) taught in Pensacola, FL where you'll learn the basic technical knowledge for cyber operations.
Advanced training in risk analysis, network traffic and security threat analysis, blue and red cell operations, and cloud security. Numerous opportunities exist for industry certifications.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an Associate or Bachelors Degree or higher may be available.

ai.blurb: Defends Coast Guard networks and the maritime shipping system from hackers, spotting and shutting down intrusions.
ai.dayToDay: Work happens at dedicated cyber shore units rather than on ships — desks, screens and secure spaces, often on shift rotations because network threats don't keep office hours. You'll be sifting network traffic, chasing anomalies, writing up findings and working alongside analysts and network defenders. Plenty of the job is patient, detailed digging that leads nowhere, punctuated by the times it leads somewhere serious.
ai.funFact: CMS trainees go through the Navy's Joint Cyber Analysis Course in Pensacola — 27 weeks, one of the longest enlisted technical schools in the US military.
goodFitIf: you enjoy picking apart technical puzzles
you notice small details others miss
you're already comfortable with computers
you can stay focused for long stretches

title: Damage Controlman
tagline: DCs are experts in welding, plumbing, and carpentry, as well as fighting fires and flooding.
overview: DCs perform the most hands-on fabrication work in the Coast Guard. You'll gain skills in welding, plumbing, and carpentry. Onboard a cutter, you'll be responsible for damage control—including systems maintenance, crew training, and rapid emergency response. Ashore, DCs serve at engineering support units and base facilities to maintain shoreside infrastructure.
requirements: Are you a hands-on person?
Are you good at building and repairing things?
Are you interested in emergency response?
Are you experienced or interested in welding, carpentry, or plumbing?
training: DCs receive a 15-week rating course in Yorktown, VA with instruction in welding; firefighting; carpentry; plumbing; chemical, biological, and radiological warfare defense; and shipboard damage control.
Advanced training in welding, firefighting, and shipboard damage control, as well as advanced CBR and non-destructive weld examination training.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Engineering Technology program is available to the DC rating.

ai.blurb: Welds, plumbs and builds aboard Coast Guard cutters, and leads the response when a ship catches fire or floods.
ai.dayToDay: Most days are maintenance and fabrication: patching pipework, welding brackets, repairing woodwork and checking that firefighting and dewatering gear actually works. On a cutter you also run damage control drills and train the rest of the crew, because everyone fights the fire but you're the one who knows how. Ashore, the same skills go into keeping base buildings and engineering support units in working order.
ai.funFact: Damage Controlmen also train in chemical, biological and radiological defence — on a ship there's nowhere to evacuate to, so the crew has to handle contamination themselves.
goodFitIf: like working with your hands
stay calm in emergencies
enjoy welding, carpentry or plumbing
want a trade that transfers ashore

title: Diver
tagline: DVs conduct searches, recoveries, investigations, maintenance, and repairs in a variety of underwater conditions across the globe.
overview: DVs are highly trained military divers. Your duties may include recovery of weapons, ship maintenance or repair, and clearing obstructed waterways. DVs use side scan sonar equipment, underwater remote-operated vehicles, metal detectors, and various exothermic cutting and hydraulic power tools. You'll be trained to succeed in waters from the pristine tropics to frigid conditions under polar ice. DVs are typically assigned to dedicated shoreside diving units.
requirements: Are you physically and mentally fit?
Are you extremely comfortable in the water?
Are you a detail-oriented person?
Are you a team player?
training: Unlike most ratings, you cannot apply to become a DV until you have advanced to E-4 in another rating. DVs receive a 21-week rating course at the Navy Diving and Salvage Training Center in Panama City, FL, with instruction in air and mixed gas diving using SCUBA and hard hat; underwater cutting and welding; recompression chamber operations; underwater hydraulic tools; ship maintenance, repair, and salvage; lift bag operations; etc.

Advanced training in cold water ice diving, along with instructor development training, EMT training, a first class diver supervisory course, side scan and remote-operated vehicle course, and various dive gear maintenance courses.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to credentials, certifications, and licenses are available. Opportunities leading to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may also be available.

ai.blurb: Works underwater for the Coast Guard — searching, salvaging, cutting, welding and repairing ships in everything from tropical water to under polar ice.
ai.dayToDay: Most DVs are posted to dedicated shoreside diving units, so the work comes in bursts: a recovery job, a hull inspection, clearing something out of a waterway. You dive in teams with a supervisor topside, using SCUBA or hard hat gear, side scan sonar, ROVs, hydraulic tools and exothermic cutting torches. Between jobs there's a great deal of gear maintenance, training and physical conditioning — the unglamorous part that keeps everyone alive.
ai.funFact: You can't join the rating straight out of boot camp: you have to advance to E-4 in another rating first, then earn a seat at the Navy Diving and Salvage Training Center in Panama City, Florida.
goodFitIf: are completely at ease underwater
stay calm when things go wrong
are meticulous about equipment checks
want to earn a rating first

title: Electrician’s Mate
tagline: EMs install, maintain, and repair sophisticated electrical equipment and machinery control systems at Coast Guard units and onboard cutters.
overview: EMs are responsible for electrical equipment, including power generation and distribution systems, propulsion motors, navigation equipment, and machinery control systems. You'll be trained in electrical theory, circuit applications, programmable logic, and fiber optics principles. At smaller units, an EM may be the Engineer Petty Officer, who is responsible for the engineering department and equipment. EMs are assigned to a wide variety of units.
requirements: Are you interested in electrical and mechanical systems?
Are you good at math or problem solving?
Are you excited to solve challenging technical problems?
Are you interested in a STEM career?
training: EMs receive a 16-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in mathematics, physics, and electrical circuit analysis.
Advanced training in analog and digital electronics, programmable logic controllers, fiber optics, gyrocompass systems, power generation and speed control, and machinery plant control.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Engineering Technology program is available to the EM rating.

ai.blurb: Keeps the electrical systems running on Coast Guard ships and shore units — generators, propulsion motors, navigation gear and machinery controls.
ai.dayToDay: Much of the work happens in engine rooms, switchboard spaces and workshops, either aboard a cutter at sea or at a shore unit. You'll be troubleshooting circuits, servicing generators and motors, and working on programmable logic controllers and fibre optic runs, usually alongside other engineering-rate Coast Guardsmen. At a small unit you could end up as the Engineer Petty Officer, meaning the whole engineering department and its equipment is your problem.
ai.funFact: Training runs 16 weeks at Yorktown, Virginia, and covers everything from circuit analysis to gyrocompass systems — the spinning instrument that finds true north without relying on magnetism.
goodFitIf: You like maths and problem solving
Circuits and machinery genuinely interest you
You want a STEM trade with civilian value
You don't mind cramped engine spaces

title: Electronics Technician
tagline: ETs install, repair, and maintain command, control, computer, communications, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (C5ISR) systems.
overview: ETs are responsible for sophisticated electronics onboard cutters and ashore, including installation and repairs of command, control, computer, communications, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (C5ISR) systems. You’ll employ a deep knowledge of electrical theory, along with practical hands-on skills to maintain systems that keep Coast Guard units on the cutting edge. ETs are typically assigned to cutters and shoreside electronic support units.
requirements: Are you interested in electronic systems?
Are you good at math or problem solving?
Are you naturally curious about how things work?
Are you innovative and analytical?
training: ETs receive a 20-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in electronic systems, navigation systems, and network integrated control systems.
Advanced training in shipboard defense systems, radar systems, electronic fundamentals, and electronic technical and engineering skills.
Cyber certification.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Cyber Technology program is available to the ET rating.

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard radar, radios, navigation and computer systems working, aboard ships and at shore stations.
ai.dayToDay: You're the person called when a radar stops painting contacts or a radio goes quiet — often at sea, often at an awkward hour. Work splits between planned maintenance, installing new kit, and tracing faults with test gear and schematics until you find the one failed component. Assignments are typically on cutters or at shoreside electronic support units, working alongside the operators who depend on the gear.
ai.funFact: ET training happens at the Coast Guard's training centre in Petaluma, California — a 20-week course covering electronic, navigation and network control systems, plus a cyber certification.
goodFitIf: enjoy tracing faults to their source
are comfortable with maths
like knowing how things work
don't mind fixing things at sea

title: Health Services Technician
tagline: HSs provide emergency healthcare to those in distress and give medical care to Coast Guard crews.
overview: HSs meet the urgent medical needs of those in distress and maintain the readiness of Coast Guard crews. You'll be trained in emergency medical care and specialties such as X-ray technician, diagnostic testing, pharmacy, and dental treatment. You may prescribe medications, administer immunizations, or perform minor surgical procedures. HSs are typically assigned to cutters or Coast Guard clinics ashore.
requirements: Are you detail-oriented?
Are you drawn to medicine or dental health?
Are you strong in STEM subjects?
training: HSs receive a 22-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in clinical laboratory procedures, sterilization techniques, preventative medicine, nursing, pharmacy, and wound treatment.
Advanced X-ray technician training, pharmacy technician training, behavioral health training, independent duty certification, and nationally registered emergency medical technician (EMT) training.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Health Care Administration and Physicians Assistant programs are available to the HS rating.

ai.blurb: Coast Guard medic who treats rescued people in distress and keeps crews healthy, afloat and ashore.
ai.dayToDay: Most days look like a small clinic: immunisations, lab work, X-rays, dental chairs, pharmacy stock and a steady queue of Coast Guardsmen needing paperwork signed off before they can deploy. On a cutter you may be the only medical person aboard, which means handling anything from seasickness to a serious injury with no doctor down the passageway. The dramatic part — treating someone pulled out of the water or off a sinking boat — is real but occasional; the routine care is the job.
ai.funFact: Experienced HSs can earn independent duty certification, qualifying them to run a cutter's sick bay alone at sea, including prescribing medication and minor surgical procedures.
goodFitIf: stay calm when others panic
like medicine and detail work
can work without a supervisor nearby
enjoy science and lab procedures

title: Intelligence Specialist
tagline: ISs turn information into actionable intelligence that enables missions to succeed.
overview: ISs connect the right information to the right person at the right time. You'll plan and execute intelligence operations to collect information from adversaries to ensure the success of Coast Guard missions. You'll use advanced technology and geospatial techniques to predict and communicate locations and actions of adversaries. ISs are typically assigned to shoreside sectors, districts, cutters, and major intelligence units.
requirements: Are you analytical with a critical thinking mindset?
Are you interested in a STEM-related career?
Are you interested in using computers and data to solve problems?
Are you comfortable keeping secrets?
training: ISs receive a 12-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in intelligence disciplines, intelligence analysis and briefing, and protecting classified information.

Advanced training in intelligence collection and analysis, counterintelligence analysis, and operations, as well as advanced training in human intelligence, signals intelligence, cyber intelligence, and geospatial intelligence.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Strategic Intelligence Program is available to the IS rating.

ai.blurb: Collects and analyses information about smugglers, traffickers and other threats, then gets it to the people who need it.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens at a desk inside a secure space at a Coast Guard sector, district or intelligence unit, with some billets afloat on cutters. You'll be reading reports, cross-checking databases, plotting patterns on maps and writing or briefing what it all means for operators planning a boarding or patrol. The pace swings between long stretches of patient research and sudden urgency when something develops.
ai.funFact: Coast Guard ISs train at Yorktown, Virginia, and can go on to the Strategic Intelligence Program 	a funded route to a degree that few enlisted intelligence jobs offer.
goodFitIf: you enjoy patient research
you can keep a secret indefinitely
maps and data interest you
you write and brief clearly

title: Information Systems Technician
tagline: ITs are system administrators that support the people and equipment required for every mission, including telephones, computers, and network systems.
overview: ITs are responsible for computer and voice networks. You'll be a system administrator for unclassified and classified systems, and manage hardware, firmware, and software to keep units' IT resources online. Aboard a cutter, you'll use your skills to support tactical command, control, and communications systems. ITs are also assigned to electronics support units, providing critical support to computer systems at various units to keep them mission capable.
requirements: Are you interested in computers, networks, or technology?
Are you a go-to electronics fixer for friends or family?
Are you excited to solve challenging technical problems?
Are you interested in a STEM career?
training: ITs receive a 28-week rating course in Petaluma, CA, with instruction in maintenance and management of computer servers and workstations, copper and fiber cable installation, network management, telephone system programming, IT system administration, and software and hardware installation.
Advanced training in telephone services such as voicemail, auto attendant, and telephone class of service modifications.

Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities leading to an associate or bachelor's degree or higher may be available. Specifically, the Cyber Technology program is available to the IT rating. Voluntary Cyber Security educational opportunities are available through Navy Community College.

ai.blurb: Keeps Coast Guard computers, phones and networks running, ashore and aboard cutters.
ai.dayToDay: You're the system administrator: patching servers, swapping hardware, pulling copper and fibre cable, programming phone systems and fielding the "my laptop won't connect" calls. Work happens at shore units, electronics support units, or aboard a cutter supporting tactical command, control and communications gear. Expect a mix of planned projects and whatever breaks that morning, usually with someone waiting on you to fix it.
ai.funFact: IT training runs 28 weeks at Training Center Petaluma in California, and the rating has its own Cyber Technology degree pathway.
goodFitIf: Friends call you to fix things
You like networks and servers
Methodical troubleshooting appeals to you
You want a STEM career path

title: Marine Science Technician
tagline: MSTs inspect vessels and facilities, and respond to pollution incidents.
overview: MSTs are specialists who enforce laws related to safety, security, and environmental protection. You'll board vessels, inspect commercial waterfront facilities, and respond to disasters that affect the environment or operation of a port. You may search containers or oversee handling of hazardous cargo to prevent disruptions to critical maritime commerce infrastructure. MSTs are typically assigned to shoreside sectors and specialized units.
requirements: Are you interested in emergency response?
Are you passionate about the environment?
Are you consistent and methodical?
Are you interested in a STEM career?
training: MSTs receive a 12-week rating course in Yorktown, VA, with instruction in investigation of pollution incidents, pollution cleanup operations, and vessel and waterfront facility inspections.
Training in container inspections and explosives handling, as well as federal on-scene coordinator representative and other national incident management system certifications.
Both full-time and part-time Coast Guard-funded educational opportunities that lead to an associate degree, bachelor's degree, or higher may be available.

ai.blurb: Inspects ships and waterfront facilities for safety and environmental compliance, and responds when oil or chemicals spill.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work is shoreside, attached to a Coast Guard sector or a specialised unit in a port town. A normal day might mean climbing around a tank barge with a checklist, auditing how a terminal stores hazardous cargo, or writing up what you found; when something goes wrong, you're on scene coordinating a pollution response with federal and state agencies and contractors. It's paperwork and regulations as much as boots and coveralls, and both halves matter.
ai.funFact: MSTs can qualify as Federal On-Scene Coordinator Representatives, meaning a fairly junior enlisted person can hold real legal authority over a spill response.
goodFitIf: you like rules and checklists
you care about the environment
you want science without a lab
you stay calm during messy incidents
